claims.text: OrderPlacedTightlyCoupled initialises its EmailNotifier field with new(); OrderNotifications takes an INotifier constructor parameter and never writes new for it.
In C# (12 and later), parameters in parentheses right after a class name are constructor parameters available to the whole class body (primary constructor).

claims.text: OrdersController's constructor takes OrderService (a concrete sealed class) and IOrderRepository (an interface).
OrderService's constructor takes IOrderRepository and INotifier, and OrderService never creates either with new.
Nothing in the samples project creates an OrderNotifications instance at stage-1.
EfOrderRepository's constructor takes DonHangDbContext, a concrete class.
DIP is the principle (depend on abstractions); DI is a technique for supplying a dependency from outside; a class can be injected with a concrete type (DI without inversion).
A class that creates its own concrete object is tied to it even if the field's declared type is the interface.
Constructor parameters are the most common way to inject a dependency in C#; other forms exist (for example ASP.NET Core action injection with [FromServices]).
